news_title: UK links Salmonella outbreak to Moroccan tomatoes
efet_title: UK links Salmonella outbreak to Moroccan tomatoes
efet_body:
The United Kingdom recorded the most infections in a multi-country Salmonella outbreak that was likely caused by contaminated tomatoes from Morocco.
Between July and October 2024, 216 patients with genetically related Salmonella Blockley infections were identified including 56 in France, 30 in Germany, and 129 in the UK. In the UK, 79 people were sick in England, 33 in Scotland, and 17 in Wales. One person in the United States fell ill but they had been to the UK before symptom onset.

news_title: New South Wales misses Salmonella reduction target
efet_title: New South Wales misses Salmonella reduction target
efet_body:
An Australian state has fallen short of its Salmonella reduction target but made major progress in reducing infections.
The New South Wales (NSW) Food Authority said an evaluation revealed that efforts had prevented more than 37,000 illnesses.

news_title: Raw Oysters Salmonella Outbreak Sickens 27 in 12 States - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Raw Oysters Salmonella Outbreak Sickens 27 in 12 States - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
A raw oysters Salmonella outbreak has sickened at least 27 people in 12 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (
CDC
). The oysters were harvested by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company from the Little Wicomico River harvest area in Virginia.
The case count by state is: Connecticut (1), Florida (1), Iowa (1), Illinois (1), Kentucky (1), New Jersey (1), Colorado (2), Indiana (2), Maryland (2), Virginia (3), New York (4), and Pennsylvania (8). The patient age range is from 1 to 86 years, and illness onset dates range from May 29, 2026 to September 14, 2026. Five people have been hospitalized because they are so sick.
This
outbreak
was first reported by the Virginia Department of Health as caused by oysters and clams harvested from that river. Pennsylvania officials notified that department in Virginia about illnesses in their state and Virginia put a temporary emergency closure from October 9, 2026 through November 7, 2026 for shellfish harvesting on the Little Wicomico River.
A
recall
was issued by the Virginia Department of Health, Division of Shellfish Safety and Waterborne Hazards for shellstock oysters. The oysters were distributed to these states: Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, North Carolina, New Jersey, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Texas. The serotype is Salmonella Telelkebir.
State and local health department agents interviewed people about the foods they ate the week before they got sick. Of 13 people who gave information to public health officials, 10, or 77%, reported eating raw oysters. This percentage was significantly higher than the 1.6% of respondents who ate rate oysters in the FoodNet Population Survey.
Then, whole genome sequencing conducted on patient isolates showed that the bacteria that made them sick was closely related genetically. This means that the patients in this outbreak likely got sick from eating the same food. Officials in Pennsylvania collected samples of raw oysters from a distributor that supplied the shellfish to restaurants where patients said they ate. One oyster sample from the Little Wicomico Oysters Company tested positive for Salmonella; testing on the serotype is pending.
Traceback was conducted for seven of the 10 people who ate raw oysters to see where they came from. Oysters eaten by sick people were harvested from multiple geographic locations, but oysters harvested from the Little Wicomico River by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company were the only oysters in common to the seven ill people included in traceback.
If you have eaten raw oysters and have been ill with the
symptoms
of Salmonella food poisoning, see your doctor. You may be part of this outbreak.

news_title: Austrian tomato warning follows Salmonella infections
efet_title: Austrian tomato warning follows Salmonella infections
efet_body:
Austrian authorities have warned against eating tomatoes from certain Italian regions because of a connection to recurring Salmonella outbreaks.
The Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES) and the Federal Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs, Health, Care and Consumer Protection (BMASGPK) said the alert covers raw cherry tomatoes from the areas of Ragusa and Caltanissetta in Sicily.
If cherry tomatoes from these regions must be used, officials said they should be thoroughly heated before consumption.
National impacts
In Austria, 21 confirmed and eight probable Salmonella Strathcona cases have been reported in seven federal states. Initial results from interviews with patients point to stays in Italy and the consumption of tomatoes.
One person was sick during the winter, and 28 fell ill from the end of July. Seven people required hospitalization. The median age of those affected is 36 with a range of 10 months to 79 years old. Patients are 17 males and 12 females. Six cases were likely infected abroad. Of these, five had traveled to Italy and one had been to Croatia prior to the onset of illness.
Earlier this month, Italian authorities found monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Strathcona in cherry tomatoes. They also reported 117 salmonellosis cases in Brescia and 15 in Bergamo.
Authorities in Puglia suspended the serving of raw fresh tomatoes in food preparation centers and distribution points for institutional catering. This includes nurseries, schools, social care and healthcare facilities, residential care homes and hospitals. The measures followed a rise in Salmonella Strathcona infections and detection of Salmonella in a batch of tomatoes from Caltanissetta.
In October, the Food Safety, Veterinary and Plant Protection Administration (UVHVVR) in Slovenia was informed that a lot of cherry tomatoes from Italy had been delivered to several catering companies between Sept. 7 and 9. The alert was raised because of the confirmed presence of Salmonella, which had caused illness in other member states. Further checks revealed all stocks had been used and were not available to consumers via retailers. UVHVVR has recorded no outbreaks linked to tomatoes since Sept 7.
Persistent, common contamination source
Since July 2026, more than 160 confirmed infections have been recorded across 10 European countries. Sequencing results are pending for 100 more patients.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the recurrence of cases suggests ongoing transmission and distribution of contaminated produce both in and beyond Italy.
“The risk for new infections remains as long as the seasonal delivery of contaminated produce continues. New outbreaks are likely to occur in future seasons until the root cause of the contamination has been identified and control measures implemented,” according to the agency.
Between 2023 and 2026, 800 people have fallen sick in 17 European countries, including 133 in Austria. Cases occur mostly from late summer through to December.
Germany experienced its largest outbreak caused by Salmonella Strathcona in the 2025-2026 season, with 116 cases. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) said recently that there are 39 patients associated with the outbreak since June 2026.
In addition to a close genetic relationship, the seasonal pattern of cases, patient interviews and food investigations support the hypothesis that outbreaks can be traced back to a common source of contamination.
In late 2025, AGES detected the outbreak strain in organic cherry tomatoes from Italy. The outbreak strain was also found in the irrigation water of a tomato producer in Sicily.

news_title: USDA to expand testing for deli meat processors - Food Safety News
efet_title: USDA to expand testing for deli meat processors - Food Safety News
efet_body:
The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service is implementing a new nationwide program for the inspection of establishments that process ready-to-eat deli meats.
The new program follows a pilot program and will require inspectors to collect food-contact and non-food-contact surface swabs in addition to product samples. The Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) plans to phase in the program across its nine districts beginning in January 2027 and running through March 2027.
“Broader sampling and more data ultimately means safer food,” according to FSIS. “The agency intends to use the resulting data to work with establishments to ensure that corrective actions effectively address root causes or harborage sites.”
The program is part of a series of changes to FSIS oversight of Listeria in ready-to-eat (RTE) facilities following the deadly 2024 Listeria outbreak traced to Boar's Head deli meat. A review of records showed that there was a history of food safety failures at the company’s Jarret, VA, production facility that went unresolved despite the fact that inspectors repeatedly found violations.
The FSIS pilot program took place in the Alameda, Chicago and Raleigh districts. Results from the pilot project have not been published.

If the sampling identifies Listeria monocytogenes, whole genome sequencing will be performed and compared to reported illnesses or other historical results.
Environmental samples have traditionally been collected as part of specialized sampling activities, typically conducted by Enforcement, Investigations, and Analysis Officers at irregular intervals. Under the new program, in-plant inspectors will collect a small number of environmental samples but at a more regular frequency.
The FSIS says the expanded sampling as a tool for identifying potential Listeria harborage sites and assessing sanitation effectiveness at individual establishments while also providing insight into Listeria trends nationwide.
Companies producing RTE products under FSIS jurisdiction are expected to take steps to prepare for the increased sampling, such as:
Evaluating the establishment’s environmental monitoring program and historical findings;
Assessing corrective action and root cause investigation practices and capabilities;
Conducting any desired program updates or self-evaluations before enhanced sampling is implemented; and
Ensuring the company has the ability understand and assess WGS results.

news_title: UK egg sampling discovers different Salmonella outbreak - Food Safety News
efet_title: UK egg sampling discovers different Salmonella outbreak - Food Safety News
efet_body:
Sampling of imported eggs as part of an investigation into Salmonella infections has uncovered a different outbreak in the United Kingdom.
The Salmonella Enteritidis strain identified in a batch of eggs from Ukraine is different to the strains linked to another Salmonella outbreak but is associated with 36 illnesses in England in 2026.
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) and Food Standards Scotland (FSS) have asked businesses, including caterers, manufacturers and wholesalers, to withdraw and recall all dates and sizes of eggs from one Ukrainian business because of Salmonella Enteritidis contamination.
Ukrainian connection
Affected eggs came from the Yasensvit company in Kyiv and are stamped with the code 3UA1012066. They may have been supplied to catering businesses or sold through smaller retail outlets. Eggs may have been repacked by UK businesses and sold under different names or packing center details on the outer packaging.
Egg sampling was undertaken as part of an investigation into a large outbreak which is thought to be linked to imported eggs. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) found Salmonella Enteritidis in samples of eggs from the Ukrainian supplier and carried out whole genome sequencing.
Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the FSA, said: “We have identified Salmonella Enteritidis in eggs that were imported from a business in Ukraine and taken urgent action to protect public health and advised that any affected product on the UK market is withdrawn and recalled.
“This issue relates specifically to eggs from one business in Ukraine, which are primarily supplied through wholesalers and the catering supply chain, but also sold at small retailers. Consumers should not eat these eggs and businesses should withdraw them, and where retail sales have occurred, recall them, as these eggs may be unsafe to eat.”
Main outbreak update
As part of three Salmonella outbreaks in the United Kingdom, more than 650 people have fallen sick and two have died.
Investigations have linked 47 patients to 11 businesses, with at least 24 infected people eating dishes containing eggs. The eggs come from multiple sources, but two large importers are being investigated further.
In the first cluster, there have been 428 confirmed patients and one death. Sample dates range from Aug. 11, 2025, to Sept. 22, 2026. In the past month, 102 infections have been reported in England.
Sick people range in age from younger than 1 to 90 years old with a median age of 30. Of 271 patients with available information, 72 have been admitted to hospitals.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is also monitoring this Salmonella Enteritidis sequence type 11 cluster. At least 34 people have been hospitalized. People fell sick in the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Denmark, France, and Germany.
In the second cluster, there are 194 patients in England. Sample dates range from May 27, 2025, to Sept. 14, 2026. Patients are aged between younger than 1 to 92 with a median of 29 years old. Of 55 patients with information available, 25 were admitted to hospitals.
In a third cluster, there are 44 cases and one death, with sample dates ranging from Jan. 27 to Aug. 24, 2026. Patients range in age from younger than 1 to 87 with a median of 32 years old. Nine people have been hospitalized.
In Scotland, there are 16 confirmed patients. Fifteen are in the first cluster and one in the third cluster reported by UKHSA. Sample dates are from April 1 to Sept. 3, 2026. Patients range in age from 2 to 78 with a median of 36 years old and 11 are female. Several people have reported bloody diarrhea but none have been hospitalized because of salmonellosis. There are two Scottish cases from 2025 in the second cluster.
Wales has 10 cases in the first cluster and two in the second. One patient in the first cluster lives in Northern Ireland. There are also two illnesses in either Jersey, Guernsey or the Isle of Man.

news_title: Sunday Edition: Cultivated meat - Food Safety News
efet_title: Sunday Edition: Cultivated meat - Food Safety News
efet_body:
Quick bites from around the food safety arena this week
Taylor Farms CEO Bruce Taylor has outlined
steps the company will take after a major outbreak of produce-related Cyclospora
this past summer. Among other actions, the company announced that it is suspending the harvest and processing of iceberg lettuce from Central Mexico for sale in the United States or Canada during the Cyclospora season, which runs from May through August each year. Taylor’s statement notes that the FDA has not yet identified a definitive source of the parasitic outbreaks that made headlines all summer.
The FDA released
a 10-point plan aimed at mitigating and preventing future outbreaks of Cyclospora contamination
. It will release an Outbreak Investigation Report, improve laboratory capacity in Mexico to test produce samples and collaborate with Mexican health officials to improve education and training for people working in Mexico’s fresh produce industry.
A new CompreHensive European Food Safety (CHEFS) database
is now available to EU states via the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The database includes almost 400 million analytical results from monitoring data on pesticides, veterinary medicinal product residues and chemical contaminants. Scientists who created the database through the HOLiFOOD project say it can be used to analyze trends, predict hazards and support early warning systems for food safety threats.
Authorities in the Puglia region of Italy have
suspended the sale of raw tomatoes in canteens after reports of Salmonella infections
. The temporary order affects the use and serving of raw fresh tomatoes in all food preparation centers and distribution points for institutional catering.
The American Academy of Pediatricians is
calling for a nationwide ban on the sale of raw milk, and raw milk products
, because of the risks that it may be contaminated with bacteria, parasites and viruses. The association says, “Evidence demonstrates the overwhelming benefits to food safety conferred by standardized pasteurization and consumption of pasteurized dairy products.”
Today’s Topic: Cultivated Meat
Eight years ago, the venture capital community was all abuzz about lab-grown meat ventures. Then the money poured in.
The Good Food Institute reported that from 2021 through 2023, cultured meat and seafood companies attracted over $2.5 billion in investment. It was likely an underestimate, as money was flowing so fast that it was hard to track.
By 2023, about half of the VC capital went to a top five that included Upside Foods (formerly Memphis Meats), Believer Meats (formerly Future Meat Technologies), Wildtype, Aleph Farms, and Mosa Meat.
Sovereign wealth funds invested government money, and Tyson Foods and JBS put up profits from their cattle businesses along with traditional VC sources.
Lab-grown meat and seafood prospects were hot.
'Escape the absurdity of growing a whole chicken'
The basic idea was to use stem cells harvested from a living animal, with slaughter claimed to be unnecessary. Instead, harvested cells would be introduced to a culture medium containing the necessary growth materials and placed in a bioreactor, aiming to produce a final product that looks and tastes similar to traditional meat.
Ninety-five years ago, when he was out of power and making an income from freelance writing, Sir Winston Churchill penned an essay titled “Fifty Years Hence,” in which he wrote:
"We shall escape the absurdity of growing a whole chicken in order to eat the breast or wing, by growing these parts separately under a suitable medium."
By 2021, the venture capital crowd was all but certain that the world Churchill predicted in 1931 was coming soon, with viable lab-grown meats reaching the market.
Startups see sudden setbacks
Just four years later, the cell-cultured meat story changed dramatically and unexpectedly, with companies announcing they would cease operations.
Cultivated pork maker Meatable, headquartered in the Netherlands, ceased operations after acquiring Uncommon Bio’s cultivated meat platform, which was meant to diversify its portfolio beyond pork and beef into lamb and chicken. The 2018 startup shut down in late 2025.
United Kingdom-based CellRev, short for CellulaREvolution, developed proprietary media additives for cell manufacturing, including cultivated meat, and announced it would shut down in late 2025 because it couldn’t meet commercial milestones in time to secure investment.
Three-year-old Netherlands-based Upstream Foods, which was to develop cultivated fish fat, starting with salmon, was also among the 2025 shutdowns because it couldn't raise the needed capital.
The closure with the biggest impact last year was clearly Believer Meats. It completed a $125 million manufacturing plant near Raleigh, NC, with high-tech bioreactors and centrifuges in a 200,000-square-foot facility that was set to become a world center for lab-grown chicken.

news_title: Oysters, clams linked to Salmonella outbreak; river closed to harvesting - Food Safety News
efet_title: Oysters, clams linked to Salmonella outbreak; river closed to harvesting - Food Safety News
efet_body:
Oyster and clam harvesting has been shut down on a stretch of the Little Wicomico River in Northumberland County in Virginia after state health officials traced a Salmonella outbreak in Pennsylvania back to shellfish pulled from those waters.
Virginia health officials closed the river to harvesting on Oct. 9, just eight days into the state's new oyster season, after an epidemiological link connected the illnesses to oysters harvested there.
The Pennsylvania outbreak has sickened at least five people so far, according to the Virginia Department of Health. The agency's Emergency Condemnation order #010A, closes downstream waters of the Little Wicomico River between a specific set of coordinates, according to the Virginia Department of Health. The closure runs through Nov. 7.
State officials said the move was made out of an abundance of caution and in direct conformance with recommendations from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the health department confirmed Friday.
Crabs and finfish can still be harvested from the affected waters during the closure, and shellfish within the closure zone are being actively tested. Officials also stressed that the harvesting closure has no impact on drinking water.
The Little Wicomico closure isn't the only one in the region right now. The health department also issued a second emergency shellfish closure on Oct. 9, Emergency Condemnation #005-083B, temporarily barring harvesting in portions of Lower Machodoc Creek in nearby Westmoreland County through Oct. 29.
While in effect, the ban makes it illegal to harvest, store, or transport shellfish from condemned areas without a special permit from the Marine Resources Commission.
Virginia's 2026–2027 public oyster harvest season officially opened across public grounds on Oct. 1, meaning the Little Wicomico closure arrived just over a week into the fall season, according to Virginia Marine Resources Commission notices.
The state's public oyster grounds produce roughly 250,000 bushels annually, backed by a replenishment program that the commission says pours between $4 million and $10 million a year into reef maintenance and shell planting.
About Salmonella infections
Food contaminated with Salmonella bacteria does not usually look, smell, or taste spoiled. Anyone can become sick with a Salmonella infection. Infants, children, seniors, and people with weakened immune systems are at higher risk of serious illness because their immune systems are fragile.
Anyone who has eaten any clams from the affected area and developed symptoms of Salmonella infection should seek medical attention. Sick people should tell their doctors about the possible exposure to Salmonella bacteria because special tests are necessary to diagnose salmonellosis. Salmonella infection symptoms can mimic other illnesses, frequently leading to misdiagnosis.
Symptoms of Salmonella infection can include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever within 12 to 72 hours after eating contaminated food. Otherwise, healthy adults are usually sick for four to seven days. In some cases, however, diarrhea may be so severe that patients require hospitalization.
Older adults, children, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems, such as cancer patients, are more likely to develop a severe illness and serious, sometimes life-threatening conditions.
Some people get infected without getting sick or showing any symptoms. However, they may still spread the infections to others.
